title: The 30-Day Plan for Becoming Better at Technical Writing
content:
Becoming a better technical writer is a practice problem: write for a specific reader, test whether the reader can act, and revise the places where meaning breaks. Thirty days is enough to build a repeatable routine, though it cannot confer expertise in every domain. The plan below uses short daily exercises and three deeper reviews. It works with software documentation, operating procedures, and technical explanations because each exercise produces something that can be checked.

Days 1–5: establish a baseline

Choose one existing document you are authorized to improve. Identify its reader, task, prerequisite knowledge, and expected result. Ask a colleague to follow it without live coaching, or perform a cold read yourself after a break. Record every point where a step, term, or outcome is unclear. Keep the original version so changes can be compared. Do not treat a quick grammar pass as the baseline; the question is whether the document helps complete its task.

On day 2, rewrite the opening to state what the reader can do after finishing. On day 3, replace vague headings with descriptive ones. On day 4, define or link unfamiliar terms at first use. On day 5, check that every link names its destination and every image has a purpose. These are small exercises, but together they expose whether the document was organized around the writer's knowledge or the reader's sequence.

Google's technical-writing course overview organizes practice around foundational writing, intermediate topics, accessibility, and error messages. That breadth is a useful reminder that technical writing includes structure and reader action, not only sentence polish.

Days 6–10: write an executable procedure

Pick a small task with a clear end state, such as configuring a local test environment or exporting a report from a sample account. On day 6, list prerequisites and permissions. On day 7, write numbered steps with one action per step where possible. On day 8, add expected results and a verification step. On day 9, describe likely errors without inventing causes you have not checked. On day 10, ask someone with the intended skill level to try the procedure in an authorized environment.

Watch where the reader pauses. A step that says “configure the service” may hide five choices; a screenshot may show a button but fail to explain why to click it. Fix the missing decision rather than adding more decorative detail. If the task cannot be tested safely, label the procedure as unverified and use an isolated sample. Do not claim that it works in production merely because the prose looks complete.

Days 11–15: explain a concept with boundaries

Choose a concept that your readers often confuse. Write a definition in plain language, then an example, a counterexample, and a short explanation of when the concept matters. On successive days, remove jargon that adds no precision, check the example against primary documentation, and ask a reviewer to explain the idea back without reading your text. If the reviewer repeats an incorrect implication, revise the explanation. A good analogy helps only when its limits are visible.

Create a small diagram when relationships are difficult to describe linearly. Give it a caption that states the point and provide equivalent information in text. The exercise tests whether the visual supports understanding rather than decorating the page. Avoid copying a vendor diagram when your own labelled explanation can convey the mechanism. Check permissions and attribution for any outside material you do use.

Days 16–20: edit for access and scanning

Read the document using headings alone. Can a busy reader find the relevant section? Make headings specific without forcing each one to repeat the title. Break long paragraphs where the topic changes. Convert a dense comparison into a table only when the columns make a decision easier; otherwise a concise list may be clearer. Test zoom and narrow width so code examples and diagrams remain usable.

W3C's writing-for-accessibility tips recommend clear headings, meaningful link text, and understandable instructions. Apply those practices throughout the document, including error messages and captions.

On day 19, examine every instruction that depends on color, position, or an image alone. Replace “click the green control on the right” with the control's actual label and describe the expected result. On day 20, test keyboard navigation of any interactive example or linked demo. A writer may not control the whole interface, but can document a blocking issue and avoid creating an inaccessible instruction.

Days 21–25: verify and maintain claims

Make a claim ledger for one document: claim, source, date checked, and owner. Prioritize commands, defaults, limits, and security advice. Follow each link and confirm it supports the sentence next to it. Separate a documented product behavior from your recommended workflow. Mark assumptions and version dependencies. On day 24, ask a subject expert to challenge the most consequential paragraph; on day 25, update or remove claims you cannot substantiate.

This is also a maintenance exercise. Write down what event should trigger a review, such as a major release, a changed API, or a recurring support question. A timeless-sounding article can still contain a versioned command. Give future editors enough context to find the relevant source and understand why a step was chosen.

Days 26–30: publish a measured revision

Use day 26 to draft a concise change summary. On day 27, rerun the procedure or reading task under the same conditions as the baseline. On day 28, get one independent review focused on missing information, not style preferences. On day 29, fix the highest-impact ambiguity and check links, headings, captions, and examples. On day 30, publish through the team's normal review process and schedule the next maintenance check. Record what was observed and what remains uncertain.

A hypothetical writer improving a deployment guide might discover that readers understand the command but do not know which account it targets. They add a prerequisite that names the environment and a verification step showing the expected resource. In a second cold read, the reviewer no longer asks about the target account but does ask about rollback. The writer records that as the next revision. This is a hypothetical example, not a reported test outcome or a promise that every ambiguity disappears in a month.

Keep the habit after day 30

Use this practical checklist for every new guide: named reader and task; prerequisites; direct answer; observable steps; expected result; verified sources; labelled assumptions; accessible headings and links; a real review; and an owner for updates. A daily word count can help you practice, but it is not the quality measure. The durable skill is noticing where a reader must guess and replacing that guess with a clear, testable explanation.
